rationale: F14 (full 829-file corpus draw, 2026-09-30): the rule for what counts as a CONTRACT PARTICIPANT in `defineProps<…>()` was 'walk to the first type_identifier ANYWHERE in the type arguments', which descends into the object literal's property signatures. A property's type is not a participant. Two corpus files exposed it in OPPOSITE directions, which is what identified it: node.vue's `defineProps<{ node: NodeShape; menuId?: string }>()` has no participant at all (the props are symbols; NodeShape is the type of ONE prop, which the delegate already publishes as a declared_type row) yet the oracle derived a contract row for it — a permanent MISSING; and menu.vue's `defineProps<{ … } & Pick<CommonProps, 'height'>>()` should name `Pick`, but the analyzer took the nested `NodeShape` while the oracle took `Pick`, so each side manufactured half of one disagreement. The correct rule descends INTERSECTION and UNION constituents and type wrappers, reads a GENERIC's own name, and STOPS at an object literal. `nodes: NodeShape[]` is the array-element case that made the old pre-order rule look plausible: an array type still sits inside a property signature, so it is still not a participant. `namedControl` is the plain named type, which must keep working — a rule that only ever returns nothing would pass four of these five assertions.

forbidRelationships.note: a PROPERTY's type is not a contract participant. Scoped to a contract-marked edge from the COMPONENT: the delegate's own declared_type row to NodeShape (sourced at the `intersect` variable, from `nodes: NodeShape[]`) is CORRECT and must survive — the first version of this row forbaded the bare target and so forbaded that legitimate row too.
